title: Lucky Seven 2 Rhode Island

lines.speaker: CHAP
lines.visual: card:Chapter Two · Rhode Island|James Fenner · Brown, class of 1789

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Providence, Rhode Island. May of 1842. The smallest state in the union has two governors at the same time, and only one of them was elected by most of the men who wanted to vote.
lines.caption: Providence, Rhode Island. May of 1842. The smallest state in the union has two governors at the same time, and only one of them was elected by most of the men who wanted to vote.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: On the night of May 17th, about three hundred men follow a lawyer named Thomas Dorr to the state arsenal in Providence. They bring cannon. The cannon don't fire. The attack falls apart.
lines.caption: On the night of May 17th, about three hundred men follow a lawyer named Thomas Dorr to the state arsenal in Providence. They bring cannon. The cannon don't fire. The attack falls apart.

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: Bears, class is in session. And today's lesson, kids, is that a revolution needs working artillery.
lines.caption: Bears, class is in session. And today's lesson, kids, is that a revolution needs working artillery.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Two governors? How does a state end up with two governors?
lines.caption: Two governors? How does a state end up with two governors?

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Hold that, Gary. To get there, we start with a man who was governor three separate times, across thirty-eight years. James Fenner. He holds three numbers on Rhode Island's list. Seven, eleven and seventeen.
lines.caption: Hold that, Gary. To get there, we start with a man who was governor three separate times, across thirty-eight years. James Fenner. He holds three numbers on Rhode Island's list. Seven, eleven and seventeen.
lines.visual: card:Fact 1 of 7|James Fenner was governor three times, so he is Rhode Island's 7th, 11th and 17th

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: James Fenner was born in Providence on January 22nd, 1771. His father, Arthur Fenner, was Rhode Island's fourth governor and held the office for fifteen years, until he died in it.
lines.caption: James Fenner was born in Providence on January 22nd, 1771. His father, Arthur Fenner, was Rhode Island's fourth governor and held the office for fifteen years, until he died in it.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: James went up College Hill to the school then called Rhode Island College. He graduated in 1789. In 1804 the college took the name of a family of Providence merchants. Brown.
lines.caption: James went up College Hill to the school then called Rhode Island College. He graduated in 1789. In 1804 the college took the name of a family of Providence merchants. Brown.
lines.visual: card:Fact 2 of 7|Fenner graduated in 1789 from the college that became Brown University

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: Ah, the Browns. Now there's a tangent. I do love a tangent.
lines.caption: Ah, the Browns. Now there's a tangent. I do love a tangent.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Take the tangent, Barnaby. In 2003 Brown's president, Ruth Simmons, set up a committee to study the university's ties to slavery. Its report came out in 2006. The Brown family profited partly from the transatlantic slave trade. John Brown defended it. His brother Moses became an abolitionist.
lines.caption: Take the tangent, Barnaby. In 2003 Brown's president, Ruth Simmons, set up a committee to study the university's ties to slavery. Its report came out in 2006. The Brown family profited partly from the transatlantic slave trade. John Brown defended it. His brother Moses became an abolitionist.
lines.visual: card:Slavery and Justice|Brown University's own report, 2006

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: To Brown's credit, it asked the question out loud. Most of the club never has.
lines.caption: To Brown's credit, it asked the question out loud. Most of the club never has.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Fenner rose fast, the way a governor's son does. He went to the United States Senate in 1805. Two years later he resigned the seat to come home and run for governor, and he won.
lines.caption: Fenner rose fast, the way a governor's son does. He went to the United States Senate in 1805. Two years later he resigned the seat to come home and run for governor, and he won.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He served from 1807 to 1811 as a Democratic-Republican. He came back for another long run, 1824 to 1831. Then he stepped away. Rhode Island seemed to be done with him.
lines.caption: He served from 1807 to 1811 as a Democratic-Republican. He came back for another long run, 1824 to 1831. Then he stepped away. Rhode Island seemed to be done with him.
lines.visual: card:Fact 3 of 7|He resigned a U.S. Senate seat in 1807 to become governor

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Now the count. Rhode Island's list starts in 1775 with Nicholas Cooke. Then William Greene, John Collins, Arthur Fenner. Arthur dies in office in 1805, and two short-term fill-ins, Henry Smith and Isaac Wilbour, each get a full number. That makes James Fenner number seven in 1807.
lines.caption: Now the count. Rhode Island's list starts in 1775 with Nicholas Cooke. Then William Greene, John Collins, Arthur Fenner. Arthur dies in office in 1805, and two short-term fill-ins, Henry Smith and Isaac Wilbour, each get a full number. That makes James Fenner number seven in 1807.
lines.visual: card:Fact 4 of 7|Rhode Island gives every stint and every fill-in its own number

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Rhode Island also hands out a fresh number every time someone comes back. That's how one man ends up with three of them. Count from statehood in 1790 instead, or skip the fill-ins, and number seven is someone else entirely.
lines.caption: Rhode Island also hands out a fresh number every time someone comes back. That's how one man ends up with three of them. Count from statehood in 1790 instead, or skip the fill-ins, and number seven is someone else entirely.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: So in Rhode Island the same guy can be seventh, eleventh and seventeenth.
lines.caption: So in Rhode Island the same guy can be seventh, eleventh and seventeenth.

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: Small state, Gary. We reuse everything.
lines.caption: Small state, Gary. We reuse everything.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Now, the two governors. In 1841 Rhode Island was still running under its colonial charter from 1663, a document signed by a king. To vote, you had to own land.
lines.caption: Now, the two governors. In 1841 Rhode Island was still running under its colonial charter from 1663, a document signed by a king. To vote, you had to own land.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Factories had filled Providence with working men who owned nothing but their labor. By the 1840s, an estimated six in ten adult white men in Rhode Island could not vote.
lines.caption: Factories had filled Providence with working men who owned nothing but their labor. By the 1840s, an estimated six in ten adult white men in Rhode Island could not vote.
lines.visual: card:Fact 5 of 7|In the early 1840s about 60 percent of Rhode Island's adult white men could not vote

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: So Thomas Dorr and his allies wrote their own People's Constitution, held their own vote, and in April 1842 elected Dorr governor. The old charter government re-elected Samuel Ward King. Two governments. One state.
lines.caption: So Thomas Dorr and his allies wrote their own People's Constitution, held their own vote, and in April 1842 elected Dorr governor. The old charter government re-elected Samuel Ward King. Two governments. One state.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The numbers tell it. In the 1840s Rhode Island had about twenty-three thousand adult white men. Fewer than ten thousand of them could vote. The rest were shut out by a rule written for a colony of farmers, in a state that was filling up with mills.
lines.caption: The numbers tell it. In the 1840s Rhode Island had about twenty-three thousand adult white men. Fewer than ten thousand of them could vote. The rest were shut out by a rule written for a colony of farmers, in a state that was filling up with mills.
lines.visual: card:The vote in Rhode Island, early 1840s|About 23,000 adult white men · fewer than 10,000 could vote

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In December 1841 the People's Constitution went to its own unofficial vote. Nearly fourteen thousand men voted yes. Fifty-two voted no. Then in March 1842, the voters who already had the vote rejected a compromise constitution, eight thousand six hundred eighty-nine to eight thousand thirteen.
lines.caption: In December 1841 the People's Constitution went to its own unofficial vote. Nearly fourteen thousand men voted yes. Fifty-two voted no. Then in March 1842, the voters who already had the vote rejected a compromise constitution, eight thousand six hundred eighty-nine to eight thousand thirteen.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: On April 18th, 1842, Dorr was elected governor, unopposed, with about sixty-three hundred votes. Two days later the charter government re-elected King with about forty-nine hundred. Dorr's men called their side the people. Dorr's critics called the charter government's harsh new law against them the Algerine Law.
lines.caption: On April 18th, 1842, Dorr was elected governor, unopposed, with about sixty-three hundred votes. Two days later the charter government re-elected King with about forty-nine hundred. Dorr's men called their side the people. Dorr's critics called the charter government's harsh new law against them the Algerine Law.

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: The Algerine Law. Named by its enemies, my friends, the way the best laws always are.
lines.caption: The Algerine Law. Named by its enemies, my friends, the way the best laws always are.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: So the guy with fewer votes stays governor, and the guy with more votes goes to prison.
lines.caption: So the guy with fewer votes stays governor, and the guy with more votes goes to prison.

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: Welcome to Rhode Island in 1842, Gary. Bring a raincoat.
lines.caption: Welcome to Rhode Island in 1842, Gary. Bring a raincoat.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Then the arsenal. Then the collapse. Dorr was arrested, convicted of treason against Rhode Island in 1844, and sentenced to life. The legislature freed him in 1845.
lines.caption: Then the arsenal. Then the collapse. Dorr was arrested, convicted of treason against Rhode Island in 1844, and sentenced to life. The legislature freed him in 1845.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Life in prison? For wanting a vote?
lines.caption: Life in prison? For wanting a vote?

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Here is where the story gets more complicated than heroes and villains. The establishment answered with its own Law and Order Party. And to lead the state under a new constitution, it brought back an old man. James Fenner.
lines.caption: Here is where the story gets more complicated than heroes and villains. The establishment answered with its own Law and Order Party. And to lead the state under a new constitution, it brought back an old man. James Fenner.
lines.visual: card:Fact 6 of 7|In 1843 Fenner returned as the Law and Order Party's governor

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: But look closely at Dorr's People's Constitution. It gave the vote to all white men. At its convention, a motion to strike the word white failed, eighteen to forty-six. The people's rebellion left Black men out.
lines.caption: But look closely at Dorr's People's Constitution. It gave the vote to all white men. At its convention, a motion to strike the word white failed, eighteen to forty-six. The people's rebellion left Black men out.
lines.visual: card:The People's Constitution|Vote to remove the word "white": 18 for, 46 against

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The Law and Order constitution of 1842 did let Black men vote. It also kept a property test for immigrants. Mostly Irish, mostly Catholic, mostly the men in the mills.
lines.caption: The Law and Order constitution of 1842 did let Black men vote. It also kept a property test for immigrants. Mostly Irish, mostly Catholic, mostly the men in the mills.

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: So the rebels shut out one group and the establishment shut out another. Nobody in that fight walks away clean, my friends.
lines.caption: So the rebels shut out one group and the establishment shut out another. Nobody in that fight walks away clean, my friends.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: That's the lesson of Rhode Island. Every side drew a line around who counted. They just drew it in different places.
lines.caption: That's the lesson of Rhode Island. Every side drew a line around who counted. They just drew it in different places.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: When the new constitution went to the voters in November 1842, it passed seven thousand and twenty-four to fifty-one. A separate question asked whether only white men should vote. The voters rejected it by about three to one.
lines.caption: When the new constitution went to the voters in November 1842, it passed seven thousand and twenty-four to fifty-one. A separate question asked whether only white men should vote. The voters rejected it by about three to one.
lines.visual: card:November 1842|The new constitution passes 7,024 to 51 · a whites-only vote is rejected about 3 to 1

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Dorr was arrested in October 1843 and tried for treason against the state. He was convicted and refused to swear an oath of allegiance. In June 1845 the legislature passed an act that set him free.
lines.caption: Dorr was arrested in October 1843 and tried for treason against the state. He was convicted and refused to swear an oath of allegiance. In June 1845 the legislature passed an act that set him free.

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: He refused to say the words. You can call that stubborn. I call it a thesis.
lines.caption: He refused to say the words. You can call that stubborn. I call it a thesis.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Fenner, meanwhile, had married Sarah Whipple Jenckes back in 1792. They had four children. He was the son of a governor, the husband of a Providence family, and a Brown man. He never had to ask permission to vote in his life.
lines.caption: Fenner, meanwhile, had married Sarah Whipple Jenckes back in 1792. They had four children. He was the son of a governor, the husband of a Providence family, and a Brown man. He never had to ask permission to vote in his life.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In 1843 James Fenner became the first governor under the new constitution. He served until 1845. He died the next year, April 17th, 1846, at his Providence mansion, which he called What Cheer.
lines.caption: In 1843 James Fenner became the first governor under the new constitution. He served until 1845. He died the next year, April 17th, 1846, at his Providence mansion, which he called What Cheer.
lines.visual: card:Fact 7 of 7|Fenner was the first governor under Rhode Island's 1842 constitution

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He is buried in the North Burial Ground in Providence, a short walk from College Hill.
lines.caption: He is buried in the North Burial Ground in Providence, a short walk from College Hill.

lines.speaker: BR
lines.say: Three numbers on the list. Ever true. Thayer out.
lines.caption: Three numbers on the list. Ever true. Thayer out.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Three numbers for one man, and for most of his life, most of his neighbors never got one vote.
lines.caption: Three numbers for one man, and for most of his life, most of his neighbors never got one vote.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Rhode Island. Keep it real.
lines.caption: Rhode Island. Keep it real.
